One of the vocalic moras of the stressed syllable receives pitch accent, phonetically realised as: a) high level or high falling on a short vowel [ˊ] ... b) low rising on a long vowel [ˇ] ... or c) high falling on a long vowel [ˆ] ... Pitch accent is contrastive, as illustrated in (1)." (p. 44) "A phonological word in Palula may carry one, and only one, accent. Phonetically the accent is primarily realised as relatively higher pitch, accompanied to some extent by higher amplitude. ... The accent-bearing unit is the vocalic mora, which means that accent can be associated with a short vowel (as in (23), or with the first mora of a long vowel (as in (24), or with the second mora of a long vowel (as in (25)." new_statements.quote: "Main stress falls on the final or the penultimate syllable of the lexical root. One of the vocalic moras of the stressed syllable receives pitch accent [...] Pitch accent is contrastive" (p. 44). "[T]he location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable. Therefore, accent in Palula must be defined as lexical." (p. 73). "Accent falls either on the final or the penultimate syllable in a non-verbal lexical stem [...]; whereas in verbal stems [...] the accent is always on the final syllable. In terms of vocalic moras, only one of the three last moras, of any lexical stem in Palula, may be the locus of the pitch accent." (p. 74)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word (bare stem or stem plus suffixes) carries exactly one accent, realised as higher pitch (with some extra amplitude) on a single vocalic mora: a short vowel, or the first (falling) or second (rising) mora of a long vowel. Its position is lexical within limits: on non-verbal stems it sits on the final or the penultimate syllable (one of the last three moras), on verbal stems always on the final syllable. Accent-bearing suffixes (plural -í, oblique -í, present -áan, infinitive -áai, etc.) remove the stem accent and take it themselves; accent-neutral suffixes normally leave the stem accent in place. Minimal pairs by accent position/mora exist (káti 'saddle' vs katí 'how many?', čúur 'four' vs čuúr 'hot fire').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; the grammar states a word 'may carry one, and only one, accent' (p. 72). The word 'stress' beyond the p. 44 summary is used only for a compound's 'primary stressed part' (p. 71) and for historical OIA accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Under certain conditions the stem accent shifts onto an accent-neutral suffix (§3.5.1, pp. 75ff., with segmental alternations, e.g. ṣiṣ~ṣiṣóom); a small class of 'accent-shifting T-verbs' (§9.3.7, p. 216); some suffix allomorphy (-áan/-éen/-áand). Morgenstierne 1941 (§9, p. 11) described stress impressionistically as falling on the first long syllable from the end, no further back than the antepenult, with no tone noticed; Liljegren's mora-accent analysis supersedes this.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stem or stem+suffixes); the p. 44 statement refers to the lexical root, the p. 74 statement to lexical stems; suffix behaviour is stated separately. Postpositions 'tend to receive stress like other free morphemes' (p. 143). Description covers both main dialects, Ashret (A) and Biori (B), with A as primary.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog phal1254 Palula = Phalura/Phalūṛa (Morgenstierne 1941) = Dangarikwar/Ashreti; Liljegren 2016 covers both main dialects, Ashret (A, primary) and Biori (B), and states the accent facts for both. The related Sawi sketch (Bashir 2003, pp. 887-889) concerns a distinct language in Afghanistan, not this key.

sources.note: §9 'Stress', p. 11: 'In most words the main stress appears to fall on the first long syllable from the end, but not further back than the antepenultima.. In some cases, however, a long penultima is stressed, even when the final syllable is long.. I did not notice any lexically or morphologically relevant tone.' Weight-based impressionistic statement from short fieldwork; superseded by Liljegren's mora-accent analysis.

sources.note: 'Pitch accent' section p. 385: 'A phonological word in Palula may carry one, and only one, accent', realised as higher pitch (and some amplitude); accent-bearing unit is the mora; 'the location of the accent within a given word is not entirely predictable.
